newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Justice joins suit on Boeing helicopter parts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Justice joins suit on Boeing helicopter parts.

text.p: The U.S. Justice Department said Thursday it has intervened in a lawsuit against Boeing Co for allegedly providing the U.S. Army with helicopters with defective parts.
It said the lawsuit, which seeks civil fraud damages, alleged that for more than seven years Boeing knowingly delivered helicopters with gears that did not meet contract specification requirements.

According to the lawsuit, the faulty parts caused the crashes of two remanufactured Chinook CH-47D helicopters. It said Boeing knew engine transmission gears had been faultily made by one of its gear suppliers under a subcontract, but sold the helicopters to the Army anyway.
The initial so-called whistleblower lawsuit had been filed against the Seattle-based Boeing by a former quality assurance employee of a Boeing subcontractor.

Defense Department investigators looked into the allegations, and the Justice Department then decided to bring an amended complaint in federal court in Columbus, Ohio. That lawsuit was filed under seal April 30, and made public Thursday.
The Justice Department said a government investigation confirmed that two gears failed in flight due to cracks and faulty manufacturing that Boeing knew about.

It said one helicopter crashed in January 1991 in Saudi Arabia after only about 56 hours of operation while the other incident occurred at Fort Meade, Maryland, in 1993. There were two minor injuries in the crashes.

The Justice Department said Boeing in its warranties assured the Army the helicopters would be free from all defects in material and workmanship for 200 hours of operation or 24 months, whichever came first. The helicopters were made at a Boeing facility in Ridley Park, Pennsylvania.

"Prime contractors, like Boeing, who do business with the Department of Defense, will he held fully responsible for knowingly using defective parts that they buy from subcontractors," Assistant Attorney General Frank Hunger said in a statement.
